target.statement: Every starting state x of an irreducible aperiodic finite Markov chain admits a strong stationary time tau satisfying P_x(tau>t)=s_x(t)for all t>=0.
target.chain_scope: Finite irreducible aperiodic Markov chain, without reversibility or laziness assumptions.
target.quantifiers: For every starting state x there exists one strong stationary time tau with P_x(tau>t)=s_x(t) for every t>=0; not a different tau for each t and not only a one-sided mixing bound.
target.source_core: Complete printed minimum-density/filling-hazard construction with independent Uniform variables and joint-mass induction; source time and quotient conventions are kept literal.
target.context_role: Section 6.7 prose is the same core and has no additional independent count.

authority_use: Fixed supplied jep221/22805 evidence snapshot only; no permanent production-pointer or commit lock and no claim about subsequent corpus additions.

entries.title_for_navigation_only: Unbiased time-average estimators for Markov chains
entries.actual_counted_assumptions: A nonnegative sequence omega(i) bounded by c log(i+2)^delta exp(-xi i), with c>0, 0<xi<=1 and delta>=0.
entries.actual_counted_target: Two explicit bounds for the article quantity bar-omega: a Gamma/logarithmic bound at 0 and a geometric tail bound at j>=0; the printed convention is 0^0=1.
entries.retained_proof_mechanism: Scaling, sum-to-integral comparison, a change of variables, the retained moment inequality, and estimates of logarithmic/geometric sums.
entries.concrete_difference: This is a deterministic estimate for a bounded sequence, not an existence theorem for a random stopping time. No stopping-time, strong-stationarity, starting-state or separation-equality assertion occurs in the counted primary or its retained proof.
entries.proposed_specialization_audit: Substituting a mixing or separation bound for omega would at most give numerical bounds on the specified sequence functional. It supplies no tau and cannot yield the exact all-time identity by a standard parameter restriction.

entries.title_for_navigation_only: Perturbation theory for killed Markov processes and quasi-stationary distributions
entries.actual_counted_assumptions: The retained self-adjoint spectral setting has a simple lowest eigenspace, gap nu=lambda_1-lambda_0>0, and bounded perturbation H with norm below nu/2; the two displayed assumptions and Weyl bound are retained context.
entries.actual_counted_target: The normalized eigenfunction perturbation bound ||phi-hatphi|| <= ||H phi||/(nu-2||H||).
entries.retained_proof_mechanism: Orthogonal decomposition of the perturbed eigenfunction, projection away from the lowest eigenspace, a Weyl gap bound, and a scalar angle estimate.
entries.concrete_difference: The counted theorem concerns stability of eigenfunctions in a killed/quasi-stationary spectral problem. Neither its statement nor proof constructs a stopping time or asserts stationary independence or exact separation tails.
entries.proposed_specialization_audit: Even a finite-dimensional reversible specialization gives an eigenvector perturbation inequality. It does not extend to all nonreversible finite chains as an optimal-SST existence theorem.

entries.title_for_navigation_only: Spectral theoretic characterisation of Markov chain convergence
entries.actual_counted_assumptions: p belongs to BV[0,infinity) intersect L1[0,infinity), and ell is a positive integer.
entries.actual_counted_target: Existence of a rational step function p_ell of width 1/ell with L1 approximation error at most ess V(p)/ell, in the article literal terminology.
entries.retained_proof_mechanism: Decomposition into two increasing bounded-variation components followed by meshwise approximation and telescoping integral bounds.
entries.concrete_difference: The actual counted unit is an analytic approximation lemma. The article title about Markov convergence does not change this primary into a general Markov mixing or SST theorem.
entries.proposed_specialization_audit: No parameter choice of a BV approximation statement introduces a chain-adapted stopping time with exact separation tail. Such a deduction would require new machinery outside this counted result.

entries.title_for_navigation_only: Non Asymptotic Mixing Time Analysis of Non-Reversible Markov Chains
entries.actual_counted_assumptions: The retained weighted-conjugation/adjoint setting uses a positive stationary weight pi, T=D_pi^(1/2), and hat-P=T P T^(-1); the conclusion is for every integer k>=1.
entries.actual_counted_target: Similarity of (hat-P^k)^T hat-P^k and (P^k)^*P^k, hence equality of the Euclidean and ell2(pi) singular values.
entries.retained_proof_mechanism: The explicit diagonal conjugation computation and the weighted-adjoint identity.
entries.concrete_difference: This is a similarity/singular-value identification, including nonreversible operators, rather than a stopping-time existence or optimality theorem.
entries.proposed_specialization_audit: Applying the similarity identity to an arbitrary finite P changes its matrix representation but does not construct any tau or imply independence at tau or exact tail equality. No stronger SST result is counted here.

entries.title_for_navigation_only: Relation between Hitting Times and Probabilities for Imprecise Markov Chains
entries.actual_counted_assumptions: A finite state space, a transition matrix T, a target hitting time tau_A, and a starting x with hitting probability p^T(x)=1; irreducibility or reversibility is not required by this statement.
entries.actual_counted_target: Almost-sure eventual hitting implies finite mean hitting time: p^T(x)=1 implies h^T(x)<infinity.
entries.retained_proof_exact_tex:
\begin{proof}
    Let $R(x)\coloneqq x \cup \{y\in \X: \exists n\in \N, \ \PP_T(X_n=y \mid X_0=x)>0\}.$ Fix $n\in \N$. Then
    \begin{align}
        1&=p^T(x)=\PP_T(\tau_A<+\infty\mid X_0=x)\nonumber\\
        &= \EE_{\PP_T}\left[\PP_T(\tau_A<+\infty \mid X_n) \mid X_0=x \right] \nonumber\\
        &=\sum_{y\in \X}\PP_T(X_n=y\mid X_0=x)\PP_T(\tau_A<+\infty\mid X_0=y), \label{rompicapo}
    \end{align}
    where we used the law of total expectation and Markov's property. It follows that, for all $y\in \X$ with $\PP_T(X_n=y\mid X_0=x)>0$ it must hold that $\PP_T(\tau_A<+\infty\mid X_0=y)=p^T(y)=1$. For the arbitrariness of $n$, we get $p^T(y)=1$ for all $y\in R(x)$.

    Fix $y\in R(x)$. Since $p^T(y)= \PP_T(\tau_A<+\infty\mid X_0=y)=1$, for all $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $m_{y,\varepsilon}\in\N$ such that for all $n\ge m_{y,\varepsilon}$ we have $\PP_T(\tau_A\le n\mid X_0=y)\ge 1-\varepsilon$ or, equivalently, $\PP_T(\tau_A> n\mid X_0=y)\le\varepsilon$.
Fix $0<\varepsilon<1$ and set $M=\max_{y\in R(x)} m_{y,\varepsilon}$. Then, by picking $n=M$, we have
\[
\PP_T(\tau_A> M\mid X_0=y)\le\varepsilon,
\]
for all $y\in R(x)$.
Let $k\in \N_0$. Then, using Markov's property, we have
\[
\PP_T(\tau_A>kM\mid X_0=x)\le\varepsilon^k.
\]
We can bound the expected value of $\tau_A$ using these tail bounds:
\begin{align*}
    h^T(x)&=\EE_{\PP_T}[\tau_A\mid X_0=x] = {\sum_{n\in \N_0}\PP_T(\tau_A>n\mid X_0=x)}\\
&= \sum_{k\in \N_0}\sum_{n=kM}^{(k+1)M-1}\PP_T(\tau_A>n\mid X_0=x)\\
&\le \sum_{k\in \N_0} M\,\PP_T(\tau_A>kM\mid X_0=x)\\
&\le M\sum_{k\in \N_0}\varepsilon^k= \dfrac{M}{1-\varepsilon}<+\infty. 
\end{align*}
\qed
\end{proof}
entries.retained_proof_mechanism: Reachable-state reduction, a finite common time horizon with uniformly small hitting-time tail, Markov iteration giving a geometric tail, and tail summation.
entries.concrete_difference: The random time is the pre-existing hitting time of A. The conclusion is finiteness of its mean, not strong stationarity or realization of the separation profile. The primary does not assert independence of X_tau and tau.
entries.proposed_specialization_audit: One may apply the result to hitting times of an irreducible finite chain. This still gives only an integrability assertion about those hitting times. Selecting a target or obtaining a stationary endpoint does not establish strong stationarity or the all-t equality; that missing construction is the MCMT target core, not a routine specialization.

entries.title_for_navigation_only: A curiously slowly mixing Markov chain
entries.actual_counted_assumptions: The binary Burnside process on C_2^n, fixed x,y, and the four coordinate counts n_ab.
entries.actual_counted_target: The displayed exact product-of-central-binomial-coefficients formula for the single-step transition probability K(x,y).
entries.retained_proof_exact_tex:
\begin{proof}
The permutations that fix $x$ can be described by $G_x = S_{n_{00} + n_{01}} \times S_{n_{10} + n_{11}}$, in which we permute the indices where $x_i = 0$ and also the indices where $x_i = 1$. Similarly, $G_x \cap G_y = S_{n_{00}} \times S_{n_{01}} \times S_{n_{10}} \times S_{n_{11}}$ is the set of all permutations whose cycles are each contained entirely within each type of coordinate. If $\sigma = \sigma_{00} \times \sigma_{01} \times \sigma_{10} \times \sigma_{11} \in G_x \cap G_y$, then
\[
    \frac{1}{|\mf{X}_g|} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{C(\sigma_{00}) + C(\sigma_{01}) + C(\sigma_{10}) + C(\sigma_{11})},
\]
where $C(\tau)$ denotes the number of cycles in the permutation $\tau$, since a binary $n$-tuple is fixed by $\sigma$ if and only if it is constant (either all $0$ or all $1$) on each cycle. Therefore, by plugging into \cref{burnsidegenerictransition},
\begin{align*}
    K(x, y) &= \frac{1}{(n_{00} + n_{01})! (n_{10} + n_{11})!} \sum_{\sigma_{00}, \sigma_{01}, \sigma_{10}, \sigma_{11}}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{C(\sigma_{00}) + C(\sigma_{01}) + C(\sigma_{10}) + C(\sigma_{11})} \\
    &= \frac{1}{(n_{00} + n_{01})! (n_{10} + n_{11})!} \sum_{\sigma_{00}} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{C(\sigma_{00})} \sum_{\sigma_{01}} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{C(\sigma_{01})} \sum_{\sigma_{10}} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{C(\sigma_{10})} \sum_{\sigma_{11}} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{C(\sigma_{11})}.
\end{align*}
Now because the generating function for permutation cycle count is given by
\[
    C_n(x) = \sum_{\sigma \in S_n} x^{C(\sigma)} = x(x+1)\cdots(x+n-1)
\]
(for example by induction, since there are $(n-1)$ ways to insert the number $n$ into an existing cycle and $1$ way to add a new cycle with just $n$), we have that 
\[
    \sum_{\sigma_{00}} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{C(\sigma_{00})} = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{1}{2} + 1\right) \cdots \left(\frac{1}{2} + n_{00} - 1\right) = \frac{(2n_{00}-1)!!}{2^{n_{00}}} = \frac{(2n_{00})!}{4^{n_{00}} n_{00}!}
\]  
and similarly for the other terms. Thus
\begin{align*}
K(x, y) &= \frac{1}{(n_{00} + n_{01})! (n_{10} + n_{11})!}  \frac{(2n_{00})!}{4^{n_{00}} n_{00}!} \frac{(2n_{01})!}{4^{n_{01}} n_{10}!} \frac{(2n_{10})!}{4^{n_{10}} n_{10}!} \frac{(2n_{11})!}{4^{n_{11}} n_{11}!} \\
&= \frac{1}{4^n} \frac{n_{00}! n_{01}! n_{10}! n_{11}!}{(n_{00} + n_{01})! (n_{10} + n_{11})!} \frac{(2n_{00})!}{n_{00}!^2} \frac{(2n_{01})!}{n_{01}!^2} \frac{(2n_{10})!}{n_{10}!^2} \frac{(2n_{11})!}{n_{11}!^2},
\end{align*}
which rearranges to the desired result.
\end{proof}
entries.retained_proof_mechanism: Stabilizer/intersection decomposition, counting binary strings fixed on permutation cycles, and the permutation cycle-count generating polynomial.
entries.concrete_difference: The counted result is an explicit kernel formula for a particular chain. It contains no optimal SST statement even for that chain, and no assertion for every finite irreducible aperiodic chain.
entries.proposed_specialization_audit: A theorem about this one structured transition matrix cannot cover an arbitrary transition matrix. Turning a kernel formula into the general filling-hazard construction would be new argument, not a standard specialization.

entries.title_for_navigation_only: Comparison Theorems for the Mixing Times of Systematic and Random Scan Dynamics
entries.actual_counted_assumptions: Orthogonal projections P_1,...,P_n on a Hilbert space, with an operator-norm gap 1-delta for either all permutation scans or one permutation scan. The retained thm:gen_gap_2 is context only.
entries.actual_counted_target: Two quantitative upper bounds on the norm of the average n^(-1)sum P_i, with gaps c(delta/(n log(n/delta)))^2 or c(delta/(n^2 log(n/delta)))^2.
entries.retained_proof_mechanism: Expand powers of the averaged projection, control products containing the required subsequence using the retained projection theorem, and use coupon-collector/binomial concentration estimates.
entries.concrete_difference: The result compares projection-product and averaged-operator gaps. Its sampling-of-indices proof does not define a chain strong stationary time or identify its tail with separation.
entries.proposed_specialization_audit: Heat-bath or scan-chain interpretations remain operator contraction comparisons for the supplied projection structure. They neither represent every general nonreversible finite chain in the required form nor add the exact stationarity-and-tail construction.

entries.title_for_navigation_only: The convergence and uniqueness of a discrete-time nonlinear Markov chain
entries.actual_counted_assumptions: A nonlinear map P:R^N to R^N satisfying the article monotonicity, non-expansion and uniform-connectedness conditions, with a finite accumulation point of centered iterates f_n=P^n f-P^n f(x_0)1.
entries.actual_counted_target: Convergence of the centered iterates f_n to the unique limit g, as stated in the retained theorem. The uncentered convergence theorem and the metric-space convergence lemma are uncounted contexts.
entries.retained_primary_exact_tex:
\begin{thm}
\label{thm:NLMC convergence 3}Let $f\in \mathbb{R}^{N}$. If a discrete-time nonlinear Markov
chain $P:\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}$ satisfies

(1) monotonicity,

(5) non-expansion,

(7) uniform connectedness,

(8) accumulation point at infinity, i.e., $f_{n}\coloneqq P^{n}f-P^{n}f(x_{0})\cdot \overrightarrow{1}$
has a finite accumulation point $g\in \mathbb{R}^{N}$, 

then $f_{n}\to g$ as $n\to\infty$
and the limit is unique. 
\end{thm}
entries.retained_proof_exact_tex:
\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:NLMC convergence 3}]
Let $\tilde{P}=P^{n_{0}}$, then $\tilde{P}$ is uniformly connected
with $n_{0}=1$, implying strict monotonicity of corresponding components (2). As $g$ is an accumulation
point, then there exist $0\leq i\leq n_{0}-1$ and a subsequence $\left\{ n_{k}=m_{k}n_{0}+i\right\} $
such that $f_{n_{k}}\to g$ and $P^{n_{k}}f(x_{0})\to a\in[-\infty,+\infty]$
as $k\to+\infty$. Divide it into two cases: $\mid a\mid<+\infty$
and $\mid a\mid=+\infty$.

\textbf{Case 1.} If $\mid a\mid<+\infty$, w.l.o.g, suppose $a>0$.

Then as $k\to+\infty$, $$P^{n_{k}}f=\tilde{P}^{m_{k}}P^{i}f\eqqcolon\tilde{P}^{m_{k}}F\to g+a\cdot \overrightarrow{1}\eqqcolon\tilde{g}.$$
By Theorem \ref{thm:NLMC convergence 2}, we have
$\tilde{P}^{m}F\to\tilde{g}$ as $m\to+\infty$ and $\tilde{P}^{k}\tilde{g}=\tilde{g}$
for all $k\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$. Then for different accumulation points of $f_{n}$,
by the non-expansion property (5), their corresponding $a$ must be
the same case.

If there are two accumulation points $\tilde{g}_{1}\neq\tilde{g}_{2}$,
suppose $\alpha\coloneqq\underset{1\leq x\leq N}{\text{max}}\left(\tilde{g}_{1}(x)-\tilde{g}_{2}(x)\right)$ $>0$.
Then $\tilde{g}_{1}\leq\tilde{g}_{2}+\alpha \cdot \overrightarrow{1}$. If there exists $x$
such that $\tilde{g}_{1}(x)<\tilde{g}_{2}(x)+\alpha$, then by the
uniform connectedness and non-expansion property of $\tilde{P}$, 
\[
\tilde{g}_{1}=\tilde{P}\tilde{g}_{1}<\tilde{P}\left(\tilde{g}_{2}+\alpha \cdot \overrightarrow{1} \right)\leq\tilde{P}\tilde{g}_{2}+\alpha \cdot \overrightarrow{1}=\tilde{g}_{2}+\alpha \cdot \overrightarrow{1},
\]
which implies $\tilde{g}_{1}<\tilde{g}_{2}+\alpha \cdot \overrightarrow{1}$ and contradicts
to the definition of $\alpha$. Hence $\tilde{g}_{1}=\tilde{g}_{2}+\alpha \cdot \overrightarrow{1}$,
which means $\tilde{g}_{1}-\tilde{g}_{1}(x_{0}) \cdot \overrightarrow{1}=\tilde{g}_{2}-\tilde{g}_{2}(x_{0}) \cdot \overrightarrow{1}$.
Then the two accumulation points $g_{i}=\tilde{g}_{i}-\tilde{g}_{i}(x_{0}) \cdot \overrightarrow{1}$
for $i=1,2$ of $f_{n}$ are the same. By Lemma \ref{lem: convergence lemma by the uniqueness},
we get the convergence of $f_{n}$.

\textbf{Case 2.} If $|a|=+\infty$, w.l.o.g., suppose $a=+\infty$.

Since $\tilde{P}(f+r\cdot \overrightarrow{1})-r \cdot \overrightarrow{1}$ is decreasing for positive $r$ by the non-expansion
condition (5), we define 
\[
Qf\coloneqq\underset{r\to+\infty}{\text{lim}}\left(\tilde{P}(f+r\cdot \overrightarrow{1})-r \cdot \overrightarrow{1}\right).
\]
As $$Qg-g=\underset{k\to+\infty}{\text{lim}}\left(\tilde{P}^{m_{k}+1}F-\tilde{P}^{m_{k}}F\right)$$
is finite by the non-expansion property (5) of $\tilde{P}$, then for
any $f\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$, we know $Qf$ is also finite by the non-expansion property.
Then $Q$ satisfies the non-expansion property (5) and constant additivity
$Q(f+c \cdot \overrightarrow{1})=Qf+c \cdot \overrightarrow{1} $.

Now we show the connectedness of $Q$. For some component $x$, positive
$\delta$ and $f,h\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ with $f\geq h+\delta\cdot1_{x}$,
since $\tilde{P}$ is uniformly connected with $n_{0}=1$, we have
\[
\tilde{P}\left(f+r \cdot \overrightarrow{1}\right)-r \cdot \overrightarrow{1}>\tilde{P}\left(h+r \cdot \overrightarrow{1}\right)-r\cdot \overrightarrow{1}+\epsilon_{0}\delta \cdot \overrightarrow{1}\geq Qh+\epsilon_{0}\delta \cdot \overrightarrow{1}.
\]
Let $r\to+\infty$, then $Qf>Qh+\epsilon_{0}\delta \cdot \overrightarrow{1}$ and $Q$ is
uniformly connected with $n_{0}=1$ and $\epsilon_{0}$.

Let $\lambda_{+}^{\tilde{P}}(f)\coloneqq\underset{1\leq x\leq N}{\text{max}}\left(\tilde{P}f(x)-f(x)\right)$
and $F=P^{i}f$, then $\lambda_{+}^{\tilde{P}}(\tilde{P}^{m}F)>0$
for all $m\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ since $\tilde{P}^{m_{k}}F(x_{0})\to+\infty$. By the
monotonicity and non-expansion property, 
\[
\tilde{P}^{m+2}F\leq\tilde{P}\left(\tilde{P}^{m}F+\lambda_{+}^{\tilde{P}}(\tilde{P}^{m}F) \cdot \overrightarrow{1}\right)\leq\tilde{P}^{m+1}F+\lambda_{+}^{\tilde{P}}(\tilde{P}^{m}F) \cdot \overrightarrow{1},
\]
which means $\lambda_{+}^{\tilde{P}}(\tilde{P}^{m}F)$ is decreasing
in $m$. Since $g$ is a finite accumulation point, for all $l\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$,
we have 
\[
Qg-g=\underset{k\to+\infty}{\text{lim}}\left(\tilde{P}^{m_{k}+1}F-\tilde{P}^{m_{k}}F\right)
\]
and 
\[
Q^{l+1}g-Q^{l}g=\underset{k\to+\infty}{\text{lim}}\left(\tilde{P}^{m_{k}+l+1}F-\tilde{P}^{m_{k}+l}F\right).
\]
Then by the monotonicity of $\lambda_{+}^{\tilde{P}}(\tilde{P}^{m}F)$,
we have 
\[
\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g)=\underset{1\leq x\leq N}{\text{max}}\left(Qg(x)-g(x)\right)=\underset{m\to+\infty}{\text{lim}}\lambda_{+}^{\tilde{P}}(\tilde{P}^{m}F)=\lambda_{+}^{Q}(Q^{l}g).
\]
Since $Qg\leq g+\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g)\cdot \overrightarrow{1}$, if there is $x$ such that $Qg(x)<g(x)+\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g)$,
then 
\[
Q^{2}g<Qg+\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g)\cdot \overrightarrow{1}=Qg+\lambda_{+}^{Q}(Qg)\cdot \overrightarrow{1}
\]
by the uniform connectedness and constant additivity of $Q$, which
contradicts to the definition of $\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g)$. Hence $Qg=g+\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g)\cdot \overrightarrow{1}$
and $Q^{l}g=g+l\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g)\cdot \overrightarrow{1}$.

Let $f^{(1)},f^{(2)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}$ and assume $g_{i}$ is an
accumulation point of $f_{n}^{(i)}=P^{n}f^{(i)}-P^{n}f^{(i)}(x_{0})\cdot \overrightarrow{1}$
for $i=1,2$. Then by the non-expansion property 
\[
\left\Vert g_{1}+l\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g_{1})\cdot \overrightarrow{1}-g_{2}-l\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g_{2})\cdot \overrightarrow{1}\right\Vert _{\infty}=\left\Vert Q^{l}g_{1}-Q^{l}g_{2}\right\Vert _{\infty}\leq\left\Vert g_{1}-g_{2}\right\Vert _{\infty},
\]
we know $\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g_{1})=\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g_{2})$. If $g_{1}\neq g_{2}$,
suppose $\alpha\coloneqq\underset{x}{\text{max}}\left(g_{1}(x)-g_{2}(x)\right)>0$.
Then $g_{1}\leq g_{2}+\alpha \cdot \overrightarrow{1}$ and $0=g_{1}(x_{0})<g_{2}(x_{0})+\alpha=\alpha$.
By the uniform connectedness of $Q$, 
\[
g_{1}+\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g_{1})\cdot \overrightarrow{1}=Qg_{1}<Qg_{2}+\alpha \cdot \overrightarrow{1}=g_{2}+\lambda_{+}^{Q}(g_{2}) \cdot \overrightarrow{1}+\alpha \cdot \overrightarrow{1},
\]
which implies $g_{1}<g_{2}+\alpha \cdot \overrightarrow{1}$ and contradicts to the definition
of $\alpha$. Then the two accumulation points are the same.

By Lemma \ref{lem: convergence lemma by the uniqueness} and letting
$f^{(1)}=f^{(2)}=f$, we get the convergence of $f_{n}$. Moreover,
the case $f^{(1)}\neq f^{(2)}$ shows the uniqueness of the limit. 
\end{proof}
entries.retained_proof_mechanism: Subsequence reduction for an iterate P^(n0), a finite versus infinite centering-level split, construction of a limiting translation-homogeneous map Q, and uniqueness of accumulation points.
entries.concrete_difference: The counted object is convergence of iterates of a nonlinear map. The conclusions do not quantify over stopping times, stationary endpoints or separation-profile tails.
entries.proposed_specialization_audit: Restricting to linear finite Markov operators can provide a convergence statement when its hypotheses hold. Convergence alone does not supply an adapted randomized stopping rule attaining separation simultaneously at all times; the entire MCMT existence mechanism would still be absent.

conclusion: None of these eight actual counted primaries, read with their retained author proofs, states or gives a standard stronger-result specialization to the general exact optimal-SST existence target. Related article titles, rate bounds, hitting-time integrability and convergence results are not counted general existence theorems.
